title: Do It for the Kids — and the Adults, Too
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien argues that most school culture systems fail because they are designed for one human — either the student or the adult — while burdening the other. Systems built exclusively for students produce aspirational expectations that exhaust adults who must improvise enforcement without tools or language. Systems built exclusively for adults produce clear procedures that manage students without forming them into community. The design move that makes culture systems hold is to explicitly name and serve both humans simultaneously, building experiences that reinforce rather than compete with each other. O'Brien walks through three concrete cases: tiered behavior systems, first days of school, and the reflection room — showing in each case what the student experience and the adult experience look like when designed in parallel versus designed in isolation. The test he offers any school leader is simple: for any given culture subsystem, can you answer without hesitation what the student is experiencing and what the adult is experiencing? Where the answers are vague or the experiences compete, the gap has been found and the redesign cycle should begin there.
points: The false choice in school culture design is student-centered vs. adult-centered; the design move that makes culture hold is to refuse that choice and explicitly build for both humans in the same architecture.

A culture system designed for the student alone produces exhausted adults who improvise enforcement; one designed for the adult alone produces managed students who experience rules without community — both fail.

The reflection room is a micro-case study in dual design: one built for the student gives space to cool down but delivers the teacher a re-entering student with no repair, no re-established relationship, and the adult carries the residue of the conflict alone.

The diagnostic question every principal should be able to answer for any culture subsystem without hesitation: what is the student experiencing here, and what is the adult experiencing here — and are those experiences reinforcing each other or competing?

First days of school are an architectural moment: the student is being taught the school's expectations through demonstration and practice while the adult is rehearsing the correction language, consequence sequence, and praise protocols — both experiences must be built into the same days, by design.
quotes: Most school culture systems fail in the same way. They are designed for one human and burden the other.

The design move that makes the difference is the one most schools never make. The student culture system serves two humans, not one, and its job is to design experiences that reinforce each other rather than compete.

The student needs a safe, predictable, affirming environment in order to learn. The adult needs clarity about what is expected, the tools to deliver it, and the support when the work is hard. Both. At the same time. In the same architecture.
The student experience: I left the room and then I came back. The adult experience: someone made a decision somewhere that I am now living with. Neither person was served. Both were burdened.

Designed for both, the first days of school are a sequence in which the student is taught the school's expectations through demonstration and practice while the adult is rehearsing the correction language, the consequence sequence, and the praise protocols on the same days.

This is what is meant by designing in relationship. Not designing six separate culture subsystems and hoping they fit together. Designing each one with both humans named explicitly, mapped honestly, and held in tension until the design serves them both.

The design move is to refuse the false choice. To build for both humans at once. To accept that culture is not something you do to students with adults as the enforcement layer, and not something you do for adults with students as the input.
